source.title: Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in Large Language Models
source.authors: Jiajia Song; Zhi-Han Guo; Jiong-Hao Lin

record.tranche_reason: It tests whether previously suppressed knowledge can be recovered by fine-tuning and instructional relearning, using accuracy and F1 rather than the attacks or measures in the cited unlearning-evaluation work.
record.gate_note: The study reports unlearning and relearning outcomes for Python MCQs. It does not test activation ablation, quantization, or prompt-only recovery. Results in Figures 4 and 5 are plotted rather than numerically tabulated; the text gives trends but not exact point values. The study's cited prior results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: An education study, not a robustness test. It unlearns Python MCQ knowledge in Mistral-7B and then relearns by SFT on the forgotten QA pairs and by coach-guided LoRA. Accuracy is measured on held-out A3 items. This bears on A (degree of forgetting, recovery by relearning) and B (relearning restores suppressed knowledge) in a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that unlearning yields controllable novice-like agents and that the degradation is 'not irreversible'. Both SFT on the forgotten QA pairs and coach-guided dialogue recover part of the suppressed knowledge, which they read as reacquisition rather than complete erasure. Recovery is incomplete, especially at 30–50% ratios. Coach-guided relearning gives steadier gains at 10–30%.
record.recipe_differences: The study adapts a targeted unlearning framework cited as Revisiting Who's Harry Potter to Python MCQs, using LoRA and an intervention-based forgetting loss. Its recovery procedures are supervised fine-tuning on forgotten QA pairs and coach-guided dialogue followed by fine-tuning; it does not reproduce the listed prompt, ablation, or quantization attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with the unlearning ratio: accuracy and F1 decline as the ratio increases, while recovery is less complete at higher ratios. Coach-guided relearning is reported to outperform static relearning, especially at moderate ratios.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Education
record.problems: All experiments use one model and Python multiple-choice questions. The paper does not report a separate retained-task/general-capability evaluation or a never-saw-knowledge comparison. Most quantitative points are available only in plots, with no exact values in the text; error bars are standard deviations across five random seeds. The dialogue example is qualitative and uses a single question.

untested.parts: General ability on a separate retained task. Chance level not stated (four options imply 0.25). No prompt, ablation or quantization attacks.
Unrelated or loosely related relearning data. A small relearning set (it equals the forget subset size). A comparison with a model that never learned the facts.

record.verdict_notes: The study's purpose is educational simulation, not unlearning robustness. All quantitative results are plotted only; the text gives just ~0.75 at 10%, below 0.5 from 40%, and base ~0.85 accuracy / ~0.77 F1. One model, one domain. The relearning set is size-matched to the forget set, so recovery cannot be separated from ordinary learning without a never-learned control. The abstract's comparison with prompt-only baselines has no reported numbers. The record's V1/V2 codes are mapped here to A/B.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures targeted-task accuracy and F1 after unlearning and reports recovery after fine-tuning, but does not establish near-chance performance, evaluate general ability on a separate retained task, or compare recovery with a model that never had the knowledge.
It tests relearning using original forgotten QA pairs and coach-generated instructional feedback. It does not test unrelated or loosely related examples.
Activation-direction ablation and analysis distinguishing blocked access from deletion are not tested.
Prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context information are not tested.
No counter-method claiming resistance to these attacks is tested.

source_check.notes: All 20 rows are figure-only (Fig 4). The text gives only base about 0.85 accuracy / 0.77 F1 and unlearned about 0.75 at 10%, below 0.5 from 40%. Fig 4 never names its eval set (A3 is the test set). Per-ratio forget-subset sizes are not stated (A2 = 903; whether 10-50% is a fraction of A or of A2 is unclear). Coach LoRA re-tests the same dialogue questions, and which items those are is not stated. Fig 4(b) legend says 'LLM Teacher'. Single model, 5 seeds.

statements.correction: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Python MCQs (16 KCs). Answer-token SFT on the full matching forget subset (A2 forget set, 903 items, accumulated in 10-50% steps) raises accuracy and F1 above the unlearned model at every ratio. It stays below base, and the gap widens at 30-50% (Fig 4, no numbers in text).
statements.problem: Groups this study under 'unlearned behaviours and multimodal knowledge return after small forget-type sets'. Its target is Python-concept MCQ knowledge in a text-only LLM, not a behaviour or a multimodal target. Relearning uses the full matching forget subset (B.against[18] says so too), not a small set. Recovery is partial and figure-only.

statements.correction: Relearned models stay below base and the gap widens at 30-50% ratios, for accuracy and more so for F1.
statements.problem: none; no numbers given, and the 30-50% gap-widening claim is in the text

statements.correction: At each ratio the relearning set is the matching forget subset (e.g. 10% unlearning then relearning on that 10% subset; A2 = 903 items). The text reports no never-learned control and no smaller relearning set.
